claims.text: High configurational entropy is responsible for the high oxidation resistance of high-temperature high-entropy alloys.
High configurational entropy produces a homogenized, single-phase microstructure.
The single-phase microstructure uniformly disperses reactive elements such as Al and Cr.
Uniformly distributed Al and Cr promote rapid formation of a continuous and adherent oxide scale.
The protective scale is primarily a composite of Al2O3 and Cr2O3.
Oxide-scale growth is intrinsically slow because the HEA has sluggish metal-cation and oxygen diffusion.
The relevant initial alloy contains multiple principal elements, including Al and/or Cr, and has a single-phase structure.
A controlled comparison can be made between the HEA and a lower-configurational-entropy alloy with similar Al and/or Cr content under identical oxidation conditions.
The proposed oxidation exposure is approximately 1100 degrees Celsius in atmospheric air for 100 hours.
The resulting composite oxide layer has limited defect density and enhanced adherence.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a homogeneous microstructure.
High configurational entropy restricts diffusion of metal cations and oxygen.
Restricted transport promotes selective oxidation of reactive elements.
An adherent, slow-growing oxide scale limits oxygen ingress and metal-ion loss, thereby protecting the underlying alloy.
Relative to the lower-entropy baseline, the HEA will form a thinner, more continuous, and more adherent oxide layer.
Relative to the baseline, the HEA will exhibit parabolic scale-growth kinetics, less spallation, and a lower overall oxidation rate.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 1000 degrees Celsius under oxidizing conditions.
The proposed mechanism requires the alloy to remain in the high-entropy regime without significant segregation or secondary-phase formation.
Specific alloy composition and processing history may modify the oxide-scale characteristics.
Failure of the HEA to form a significantly thinner, more uniform, and more adherent scale, or observation of oxidation kinetics similar to or worse than the control, would reject the hypothesis.
